etymology: From Hebrew chelbenāh, a bitter, pungent gum-resin bled from a Persian umbellifer; a KJV hapax, named once only, among the sweet spices of the holy incense (Exo 30:34).
biblical_def: Galbanum is one of the four sweet spices the LORD commanded for the perfume of the sanctuary: “Take unto thee sweet spices, stacte, and onycha, and galbanum; these sweet spices with pure frankincense” (Exo 30:34). It is a word that occurs but once in all Scripture, and that is fitting, for galbanum by itself is no sweet thing at all. Left alone its odour is bitter and rank, the sap of a rough desert plant; yet the apothecary was commanded to temper it “together, pure and holy” (Exo 30:35), and in the compound its very sharpness fixes and deepens the fragrance of the whole. The confection was beaten small and set “before the testimony in the tabernacle of the congregation” (Exo 30:36), most holy, and it typifies the prayers of the saints ascending at the golden altar (Rev 8:3). Let the reader mark the mercy in the recipe: the LORD would have a bitter gum in His holy perfume. So He gathers into the communion of saints the sharp and the sorrowful, the afflicted and the plain, and by the tempering of His Spirit their very griefs are made to sweeten the incense of the church. What is bitter alone is precious in the compound, when the great Apothecary mingles it.
webster_summary: A bitter gum-resin, one of the four sweet spices of the holy incense, named but once in all Scripture.

corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a bitter spice, galbanum recovers the truth that the LORD would have the sharp and sorrowful mingled into His holy fragrance.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation galbanum rebukes is the age’s craving for the smooth and the sweetened — the refusal of anything bitter, sharp, or hard in worship and in life. Men would strain out every pungent thing, and so lose the very note that fixes the fragrance; a religion of nothing but honey turns cloying, and a fellowship that will bear no bitter member soon has no depth of savour at all.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the wisdom of the great Apothecary, who mingles bitter with sweet by design. Galbanum alone is rank; tempered pure and holy it perfects the perfume of the sanctuary. So the LORD gathers the afflicted into the communion of prayer, and by His Spirit makes their griefs to sweeten the incense that rises before the testimony.

etymology: From Hebrew shechēleth (the KJV following the Greek onycha, a fingernail or claw), the aromatic operculum of a marine shell; a hapax, named once among the sweet spices of the holy incense (Exo 30:34).
biblical_def: Onycha is the second of the four sweet spices appointed for the perfume of the sanctuary: “Take unto thee sweet spices, stacte, and onycha, and galbanum; these sweet spices with pure frankincense” (Exo 30:34). Like its fellow ingredients it is named but once. The ancients drew it from a shellfish of the eastern seas — the closing plate of a sea-creature’s house, an unlikely thing to burn as a sweet savour before the LORD. Yet ground and tempered by the apothecary “together, pure and holy” (Exo 30:35), it gave its fragrance in the fire. The confection was beaten very small and laid up “before the testimony” (Exo 30:36), and a censer of that sweet incense, beaten small, went in with the high priest within the vail on the day of atonement (Lev 16:12). Let the reader see the pattern of grace: the LORD takes what is hidden, humble, and drawn up from the deep, and makes it holy for His presence. Onycha never sang and never shone; it was a shell out of the sea. But the fire found its fragrance. So the Lord is pleased to take the obscure and the lowly of His people and, in the tempering of His Spirit, to make them a sweet savour of Christ unto God.
webster_summary: An aromatic shell-derived spice, one of the four ingredients of the holy incense, named once in all Scripture.

corruption_summary: Not a doctrine in dispute but a hidden spice, onycha recovers the truth that the LORD makes the lowly and obscure a sweet savour before Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation onycha rebukes is the contempt for small and hidden things — the age that prizes only the conspicuous, the loud, the visible, and despises whatever is drawn up humble and obscure. A shell from the sea seems a mean thing to lay before God; and so the world reckons the quiet saint, the unnoticed servant, the hidden labour of prayer. But the LORD does not weigh His incense as men weigh fame.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that holiness is conferred, not native: onycha never shone, yet the fire found its fragrance and the priest bore it within the vail. So the Lord takes the lowly of His people and makes them a sweet savour of Christ unto God (2Co 2:15), and the hidden man of the heart is in His sight of great price.

etymology: From Greek staktē (a dropping, that which oozes), rendering Hebrew nātāph, a drop; the first-named of the sweet spices of the holy incense, a KJV hapax (Exo 30:34).
biblical_def: Stacte heads the list of the four sweet spices appointed for the sanctuary perfume: “Take unto thee sweet spices, stacte, and onycha, and galbanum; these sweet spices with pure frankincense” (Exo 30:34). The name means a drop, for it is the pure resin that oozes of its own accord from the wounded tree — the freest and finest myrrh, gathered not by crushing but by the tree’s own weeping. It is named once only in Scripture, and it stands first. Tempered by the apothecary “together, pure and holy” (Exo 30:35), beaten very small and set “before the testimony” (Exo 30:36), it rose in the sweet savour that typifies the prayers of all saints at the golden altar (Rev 8:3). Let the reader mark that the sweetest spice is the freely-flowing drop from a wounded stem. Here is the gospel figure hidden in the recipe: the fragrance most acceptable to God comes from a tree that bleeds, offered willingly and not by constraint. So the incense of the church is the free obedience of a wounded and willing heart, and above all it points to Him whose own free offering, poured out unto death, is the sweet-smelling savour in which His people are accepted.
webster_summary: The freely-dropping finest myrrh, first of the four sweet spices of the holy incense, named once in Scripture.

corruption_summary: Not a disputed doctrine but a dropping spice, stacte recovers the truth that the sweetest offering is the free gift of a willing, wounded heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation stacte rebukes is the giving that is wrung and grudging — worship offered by constraint, obedience squeezed out under pressure, the heart that must be crushed before it yields anything to God. The age has much religion of the forced sort, done to be seen or done to be safe; but the sweetest myrrh is the drop that flows of itself, and God loveth a cheerful giver.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the freeness of true sacrifice. Stacte is gathered from a tree that weeps willingly, and it typifies the offering poured out not of necessity but of love. So the acceptable incense of the church is a free obedience, and its ground and pattern is the Lamb whose own willing offering unto death is the sweet-smelling savour wherein the saints are accepted (Eph 5:2).

etymology: From Hebrew qiddāh (also qetsīāh in Psalm 45), an aromatic bark akin to cinnamon; one of the principal spices of the holy anointing oil (Exo 30:24).
biblical_def: Cassia is a sweet, cinnamon-like bark, one of the four principal spices the LORD appointed for the holy anointing oil: “And of cassia five hundred shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary, and of oil olive an hin” (Exo 30:24). With myrrh, sweet cinnamon, and sweet calamus it was compounded into the oil that consecrated the tabernacle, its vessels, and Aaron and his sons to the priesthood. Cassia was a costly article of the ancient trade, carried to and fro in the fairs of Tyre with bright iron and calamus (Eze 27:19); yet its highest use was not commerce but consecration. The word rises again in the great psalm of the King: “All thy garments smell of myrrh, and aloes, and cassia, out of the ivory palaces, whereby they have made thee glad” (Psa 45:8). There the anointing spice becomes the very fragrance of the royal Bridegroom, the Christ who loves righteousness and hates wickedness, and is therefore anointed “with the oil of gladness above thy fellows” (Psa 45:7). Let the reader join the two texts: what perfumed the priesthood at the tabernacle door now breathes from the garments of the enthroned King. Cassia teaches that the same holy anointing which set apart shadows has come to rest in fulness upon Christ, and from Him is shed abroad upon all His members.

corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a consecrating spice, cassia recovers the truth that the anointing which sanctified the shadows rests in fulness on Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation cassia rebukes is the love of the fragrant thing for trade’s sake rather than the LORD’s — the age that prizes the costly spice in the market and forgets it was first appointed for consecration. Tyre trafficked in cassia and calamus and grew rich; but the same bark, in the hand of Moses, was for a holy anointing oil, and it is a poor exchange to sell for gain what God set apart for His presence.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the unbroken line from the tabernacle door to the throne: the spice that perfumed Aaron’s consecration breathes from the garments of the King who loves righteousness. The holy anointing was a shadow; the substance is Christ, anointed with the oil of gladness above His fellows, and from Him the fragrance is shed abroad upon every member of His body.

etymology: From Latin calamus, a reed (Greek kalamos), rendering Hebrew qāneh, the sweet cane; a fragrant reed among the principal spices of the holy anointing oil (Exo 30:23).
biblical_def: Calamus is the sweet cane, an aromatic reed numbered among the principal spices of the holy anointing oil: “and of sweet calamus two hundred and fifty shekels” (Exo 30:23). With myrrh, sweet cinnamon, and cassia it was compounded into the ointment that hallowed the tabernacle and its priests. The plant is a jointed reed whose crushed pith yields a warm, spicy fragrance, and Scripture reckons it among the choicest growths of the garden of the beloved: “Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices” (Son 4:14). Like cassia it passed through the great markets, bought and sold in the fairs of Tyre (Eze 27:19). But the prophets remembered its true end and mourned its abuse: “To what purpose cometh there to me incense from Sheba, and the sweet cane from a far country? your burnt offerings are not acceptable” (Jer 6:20). There the LORD refuses the sweet cane when the heart is far from Him. Let the reader mark the lesson: the costliest spice, fetched from a far country and poured out in worship, is nothing to God without obedience. The calamus was given to anoint the holy things; it cannot anoint a rebel heart, for the LORD desireth truth in the inward parts and not the mere scent of religion.
webster_summary: The sweet cane, a fragrant reed among the principal spices of the holy anointing oil, refused by God when the heart rebels.

corruption_summary: Not a disputed doctrine but a fragrant reed, calamus recovers the truth that the costliest worship is refused where obedience is wanting.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation calamus rebukes is the substitution of scent for substance — the notion that God can be bought with the costly and the fragrant while the heart stays far off. Jerusalem sent for the sweet cane from a far country and reckoned her worship rich; the LORD answered, to what purpose? The age still trusts the outward performance, the imported and expensive gesture of religion, and still hears the same question.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that obedience is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. Calamus was given to anoint the holy things, not to perfume a rebel; God desireth truth in the inward parts. Where the heart is His, the least offering is a sweet savour; where it is not, the sweet cane from Sheba is refused.

etymology: An older English spelling of camphor, here rendering Hebrew kōpher, the henna shrub, whose fragrant white flower-clusters perfumed the ancient gardens; twice named, both in the Song of Solomon.
biblical_def: Camphire is the henna, a shrub of the eastern gardens whose thick clusters of cream-white blossoms breathe a heavy sweetness. The word occurs but twice, both in the Song, and both from the mouth of the bride concerning her beloved: “My beloved is unto me as a cluster of camphire in the vineyards of Engedi” (Son 1:14). Again it is reckoned among the choice plants of the beloved’s garden: “camphire, with spikenard” (Son 4:13). Let the reader hear the figure without straining it. The Song is a marriage-song, and the church has ever read in its bridegroom a picture of Christ and in its bride a picture of His people. Christ is to His own a cluster of camphire — not a single flower but a whole clustered fragrance, gathered sweetness, an abundance of loveliness in one Person; and this in the vineyards of Engedi, a green place in a wilderness, so that His beauty is found where the world is barren. He is the rose of Sharon and the lily of the valleys (Son 2:1), and the bride’s verdict upon Him is plain: “yea, he is altogether lovely” (Son 5:16). Camphire teaches the soul to prize Christ not by parts but as a cluster — every excellency met and heaped in Him, one sweet-smelling savour that a wilderness heart may hold to itself and be glad.
webster_summary: The henna shrub of the eastern gardens, twice named in the Song as a cluster of fragrance figuring the altogether-lovely Beloved.

corruption_paragraphs: The temptation camphire rebukes is the divided and partial love of Christ — the heart that admires one excellency in Him and passes by the rest, taking a single flower where God has given a whole cluster. The age likes a Christ of its own trimming, a bloom or two to suit the taste; but the bride will not so cheapen her Beloved. He is not a flower but a fragrance heaped together, and He is to be loved whole.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the entire loveliness of Christ. Let the soul say with the bride, He is altogether lovely; this is my beloved, and this is my friend.

etymology: The KJV rendering of Hebrew tāchash, a durable hide (whether of badger, seal, or dolphin the ancients disputed); the tough outmost covering of the tabernacle and its holy vessels.
biblical_def: Badgers’ skins are the rugged outermost covering of the tabernacle, the weatherproof hide that shielded the sanctuary and, in transit, wrapped its holy vessels. Among the freewill offerings the people brought “rams’ skins dyed red, and badgers’ skins, and shittim wood” (Exo 25:5); and the LORD commanded “a covering for the tent of rams’ skins dyed red, and a covering above of badgers’ skins” (Exo 26:14). When the camp journeyed, the ark itself was hidden beneath “the covering of badgers’ skins” (Num 4:6). This was the layer the wilderness saw. The gold and the cherubim, the blue and purple and scarlet, were all within; without was only a coarse, dark, unlovely hide, so that a passing eye beheld nothing to admire. Herein is a deep figure of Christ, of whom Isaiah wrote, “there is no beauty that we should desire him” (Isa 53:2). The world looked on the incarnate Lord and saw a plain hide, a Man of no form nor comeliness; the glory was within, veiled from careless eyes and shown only to faith. Yet the same badgers’ skin was a garment of grace to the redeemed: “I clothed thee also with broidered work, and shod thee with badgers’ skin” (Eze 16:10). What covers the holy also shod the bride; the humble hide that hid the glory is the very covering the LORD puts upon His people.
webster_summary: The tough outmost hide covering the tabernacle and its vessels — plain without, hiding glory within, a figure of the unbeautied Christ.

corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a plain hide, badgers’ skins recover the truth that God veils His glory under the unlovely and reveals it only to faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation badgers’ skins rebuke is the judgment by appearances — the age that will not look past a plain surface and so despises what it cannot admire. The world walked by the tabernacle and saw a coarse dark hide; it walked by the Son of God and saw no form nor comeliness. Men still weigh worth by the outmost skin, and so still miss the glory that faith alone is given to see.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God hides His holiest things under an unbeautied covering. Within the badgers’ skin lay the gold and the cherubim; within the plain Man of Nazareth dwelt all the fulness of the Godhead. Faith looks through the hide to the glory, and the same humble covering that veiled the ark the LORD lays as grace upon His bride.

etymology: The KJV rendering of Hebrew ōrōth ’ēlīm me’oddāmīm, rams’ skins dyed red; the crimson-dyed leather covering laid over the tabernacle beneath the badgers’ skins.
biblical_def: Rams’ skins dyed red are the blood-coloured covering of the tabernacle, the layer laid over the tent beneath the outmost badgers’ skins. The people brought them among their freewill offerings: “rams’ skins dyed red, and badgers’ skins, and shittim wood” (Exo 25:5), and again the phrase recurs in the record of the willing-hearted (Exo 35:7). The LORD commanded them into place: “a covering for the tent of rams’ skins dyed red” (Exo 26:14); and when the work was finished it was delivered up, “the covering of rams’ skins dyed red” (Exo 39:34). Let the reader mark the beast and the colour together. It is the ram — the animal of consecration, the ram of Aaron’s ordination and the ram caught in the thicket in Isaac’s stead — and its skin is dyed red, the colour of blood. So the very roof of the dwelling of God preached the gospel: the house is covered by a substitute, and the substitute is under blood. The whole sanctuary sheltered beneath a slain ram’s crimson hide, as the church shelters beneath the blood of Christ, the Lamb consecrated and slain. Above lay the plain badgers’ skin the world could see; beneath it, unseen but bearing all the weather, was the red covering — and it is the blood, hidden from the careless eye, that truly keeps the house of God.

corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a crimson covering, rams’ skins recover the truth that the house of God is sheltered by blood, hidden but bearing all.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation rams’ skins rebuke is the bloodless religion of the age — the worship that would keep the tent and the beauty within while doing away with the red covering, ashamed of substitution and offended by the blood. But strip the crimson hide from the roof and the sanctuary stands unsheltered; a house of God without atoning blood is open to every storm of wrath.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the covering of the church is the blood of a slain substitute. The ram of consecration, dyed red, was laid over the dwelling of God; and beneath the plain hide the world could see, it was the hidden blood that truly kept the house. So the saints are sheltered, not by anything the eye admires, but by the blood of Christ, unseen by the careless yet bearing all the weather of judgment.

etymology: From Old French vermeillon (from Latin vermiculus, a little worm yielding a red dye), a brilliant red pigment; twice named in Scripture, both of painted worldly show.
biblical_def: Vermilion is a vivid red pigment, and both times Scripture names it the word carries a reek of vanity and idolatry. It paints the palace of a wicked king: Jehoiakim, who “saith, I will build me a wide house and large chambers, and cutteth him out windows; and it is cieled with cedar, and painted with vermilion” (Jer 22:14). He robbed his workmen of their wages (Jer 22:13) and lavished the plunder on cedar and paint, and the LORD asked him plainly, “Shalt thou reign, because thou closest thyself in cedar?” (Jer 22:15). The second occurrence is fouler still: Oholibah’s eye was caught by “the images of the Chaldeans pourtrayed with vermilion” (Eze 23:14), and by that painted show she was drawn into spiritual whoredom. Here is a genuine and living corruption, needing no softening. Vermilion is the age’s gospel of surface — the bright coat of paint that flatters the eye and hides the rot, luxury built by injustice, and beauty made a bait to idolatry. It despises righteousness while it worships appearance; it will pay for pigment what it will not pay its labourers. Let the reader see the two houses side by side: the tabernacle, whose glory was hidden under a plain dark hide, and Jehoiakim’s hall, all cedar and vermilion without and oppression within. God covers His holiest with a badger’s skin; the world paints its emptiness bright red.
webster_summary: A brilliant red pigment, twice named in Scripture for painted worldly show — luxury built by injustice and beauty made a bait to idolatry.

corruption_summary: A genuine live corruption: vermilion is the painted show that despises righteousness — luxury built by injustice and beauty made a lure to idolatry.
corruption_paragraphs: Both times the word appears it names sin, and the age has only made the sin louder. Vermilion is the bright coat of paint over a rotten wall — the curated surface, the gilded image, the house made wide and windowed and cieled with cedar while the workmen go unpaid. Jehoiakim thought to reign by his paint; the LORD counted his splendour woe. The world still measures greatness by the finish of the façade and asks nothing of the justice beneath it.

It is worse than vanity, for painted show becomes a bait to idolatry. Oholibah saw the Chaldeans pourtrayed in vermilion and doted upon the image; the bright pigment on the wall drew her heart into whoredom. So the eye is captured by the portrayed and the polished, and the affections follow the paint into false worship. Set the two houses side by side and choose: God hides His holiest under a plain badger’s skin, but the world paints its emptiness red and calls it glory.

etymology: The KJV rendering of Hebrew sōleth, the finest wheaten meal, sifted free of bran and coarseness; the appointed substance of the meat (meal) offering.
biblical_def: Fine flour is the finest wheaten meal, ground small and sifted clean, and it is the appointed matter of the meat offering — the meal offering of the sanctuary: “when any will offer a meat offering unto the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour; and he shall pour oil upon it, and put frankincense thereon” (Lev 2:1). It was no coarse or common meal, but flour without lump or grit, evenly milled to a uniform sweetness. It accompanied the daily lamb (Exo 29:40) and filled the silver chargers of the princes’ offering, “full of fine flour mingled with oil for a meat offering” (Num 7:13). The meat offering had no blood; it was the offering of a life given wholly to God in unbroken obedience, and its substance preaches Christ. He is the true fine flour — a manhood perfectly even, no coarse grain of sin, no lump of self-will, ground small in suffering yet sifted clean, of one uniform holiness throughout. The oil poured on Him is the anointing Spirit; the frankincense is the sweet savour of His life Godward. Yet the same fine flour is found in the merchandise of fallen Babylon (Rev 18:13), traded as a luxury with the souls of men — a warning that what God appointed for pure worship the world will always seek to buy and sell. In the sanctuary it is Christ offered; in Babylon it is Christ made merchandise.

corruption_summary: Not a doctrine in dispute but a sifted meal, fine flour recovers the evenness of Christ’s holy manhood — and warns against making Him merchandise.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation fine flour rebukes is the tolerance of coarseness — the age’s ease with a lumpy, half-sifted holiness, a self-will left in the meal, a grit of sin unground. The meat offering would have nothing coarse in it; God’s eye passed over every particle. But there is a second and sharper corruption, named plainly in Babylon’s cargo, where fine flour is sold for gain alongside the souls of men — the making of holy things into merchandise.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the even, entire holiness of Christ, the true fine flour, ground small in His sufferings yet sifted of all sin, of one uniform sweetness throughout. Let the worshipper bring nothing coarse to God, and let the church beware Babylon’s traffic, which prices what heaven appointed for pure worship. In the sanctuary the fine flour is Christ offered; in Babylon it is Christ made merchandise.
